lesson: Cream stock, high-contrast Didone nameplate, tiny red section labels. Four teasers across the top with page numbers, four across the bottom, one big illustrated dossier in the middle. Everything sits on hairline rules.
steal: Teaser strips top AND bottom, each with a red section label and a page number
Line-drawing + watercolour wash instead of photography
Red used only for labels and folios, never for decoration

lesson: Same page, finished. The illustration now bleeds edge to edge behind the headline and the paper's own front page appears inside the drawing. The masthead breathes more.
steal: Full-bleed illustration with the headline sitting INSIDE it, top-left
The paper drawn into its own illustration — a wink the reader finds later
Kicker (DOSSIER) in red above a two-size headline

lesson: A modern newspaper that is unmistakably a newspaper. Sans nameplate, one spot colour per issue, flat duotone illustration, tiny type, enormous white space.
steal: ONE spot colour per issue, changed issue to issue — our department inks could work this way
Three teasers in a row under the nameplate, each with an icon
Modern without being cold — the illustrations carry all the warmth

lesson: THE closest reference for The Reading. Left page: contents list with coloured section labels, then a drop-cap essay in narrow columns. Right page: a section-coloured headline, a duotone illustration, five dense columns.
steal: Coloured section word in the folio line, top outer corner
Contents as a coloured list — section name, sentence, page number
Duotone illustration in the section ink — cheap, striking, never AI-looking
Byline in caps between two rules under the headline

lesson: One idea, one illustration, one enormous headline set INSIDE the picture. The body doesn't start until halfway down the page.
steal: Headline placed inside the illustration, not above it
A single deck of 2-3 lines, centred, doing the work of a whole intro
Two columns of justified serif with a drop cap — restful, not dense

lesson: Coloured teaser cards under the nameplate. Useful as a caution: the colour blocks are decoration, not information, and it reads as a template.
steal: The three-card teaser rhythm is good
AVOID: colour applied as a background block behind text with no reason. This is the look we are trying not to have.

lesson: A single huge illustration owns two thirds of the page, then the story starts in a white box floated on top of it. Right rail of small teasers runs the full height.
steal: Article body in a white panel floating ON the illustration
A narrow right rail of three teasers, each with a bold hed and four lines
Confidence to give most of the front page to one image

lesson: Left page is a full poster. Right page is dense text plus a vertical rail of small classified ads. Loud facing quiet — the spread logic we should use everywhere.
steal: ONE loud page facing ONE dense page. Never two loud, never two quiet.
Section slug with a fraction — 'culturas. 1/2' — tells you where you are in the section
A rail of small boxed ads down the outer edge

lesson: A brand newspaper that stays funny without becoming a joke. Heavy condensed caps headlines, double rules, playful bylines, real product photography.
steal: Condensed caps headline stack — huge impact in very little width
Double rule under the nameplate with a strapline on each side
Joke bylines that never break the format

lesson: The single best reference here for what BTS should feel like. A flat coral field, one illustration, two stacked headlines with drop caps, a narrow opinion rail, and a question set quietly into the artwork.
steal: FLAT COLOUR FIELD as the page background, illustration drawn over it
Two stories sharing one image, each with its own drop cap
A question set in a lighter tint inside the illustration — a rest stop for the eye
Left rail: label, BY line, italic bio, 'Continued on Page 6'

lesson: How to make a LIST beautiful. An illustrated scene, a giant numeral locked into it, then genuinely dense listings underneath in five columns.
steal: A giant numeral inside the illustration as the entry point
Pill-shaped category labels (FICTION) breaking the listing into sections
Dense is fine when the top of the page gave the eye somewhere to rest

lesson: Illustration as a band across the top AND a band across the bottom, with a column of text between them. The headline sits in the middle of the page, not the top.
steal: Two illustration bands sandwiching the text — completely different rhythm to a single hero image
Headline dropped into the MIDDLE of the page
Nameplate word cropped by the illustration — confident, modern

lesson: A cut-out object laid diagonally across the page, breaking the column grid, with text wrapping around it. The diagonal is what makes it feel alive.
steal: A diagonal object that breaks the grid — the grid is stronger for being broken once
Small locator map inset bottom-left
Text wrapping tight to an irregular silhouette

lesson: Cut-out player on a flat team-colour field, huge stacked caps headline in the negative space. A stats rail down the right.
steal: Cut-out figure on a flat colour field, headline stacked in the empty half
A vertical stats/facts rail — our sports page can use this exactly
Team colours as the whole palette of the page
